stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.2pa.justification: The target quantifies over exactly the four lattice points in the blueprint and sums `spt.sign` over `LGV1.signedIpats2 A A' B B'`. By definition, this set is `{spt | spt.isIntersecting}`, where intersection means the two paths share a vertex, and `SignedPathTuple2.sign` is `1` for destinations `(B,B')` and `-1` for `(B',B)`, matching the informal `\mathcal X` and sign convention. The binder `(hfin : (LGV1.signedIpats2 A A' B B').Finite)` is an encoding needed to convert the set to the finite set `hfin.toFinset`; it does not impose a genuine restriction here. Paths are finite lists of only east and north steps with fixed endpoints, so for any fixed endpoints there are only finitely many such step sequences, hence finitely many signed intersecting tuples. Thus the conclusion `∑ spt ∈ hfin.toFinset, spt.sign = 0` expresses the stated cancellation sum.

The two declarations exactly match the two blueprint equalities. `sum_signedPathTuples2` states that the signed sum over `signedPathTuples2 ... = Set.univ` is `↑(numPaths A B) * ↑(numPaths A' B') - ↑(numPaths A B') * ↑(numPaths A' B)`, i.e. the number of tuples to `(B,B')` minus the number to `(B',B)`. `sum_signedNipats2` sums over `signedNipats2 ... = {spt | ¬ spt.isIntersecting}` and equates it to `↑(numNipats2 A A' B B') - ↑(numNipats2 A A' B' B)`, exactly the corresponding nipat difference. The sign definition, `if spt.toBB' = true then 1 else -1`, agrees with the informal sign convention. The binders `hfin : (...).Finite` are an encoding requirement for forming `hfin.toFinset`, not a mathematically contentful restriction: with east/north finite step lists and fixed endpoints, these path-tuple sets are finite. Reversing the order of the first displayed blueprint equality (count difference equals sum versus sum equals count difference) is immaterial by symmetry of equality.

The formal declarations collectively imply the blueprint claim. The domain is exactly the intersecting signed path tuples: `∀ {A A' B B'} (spt : SignedPathTuple2 A A' B B') (h : spt.isIntersecting)`, where `isIntersecting` is `∃ v ∈ spt.path0.vertices A, v ∈ spt.path1.vertices A'`, matching “the paths p and p' have a vertex in common.” The body of `ipatInvolution` chooses `firstIntersection spt h`, splits both step lists with `List.take`/`List.drop` at its first occurrence, forms `head0 ++ tail1` and `head1 ++ tail0`, and flips `toBB'`, exactly implementing the prescribed tail exchange and corresponding sign swap. Closure on the set X is supplied by `ipatInvolution_isIntersecting`: `(ipatInvolution spt h).isIntersecting`. The involution property is supplied by `ipatInvolution_involutive`: `∃ (h' : spt'.isIntersecting), ipatInvolution spt' h' = spt`; proof irrelevance makes the proof argument immaterial, so this yields the required self-inverse map on intersecting tuples. Finally, `ipatInvolution_sign` states `(ipatInvolution spt h).sign = -spt.sign`, with `sign` defined to be `1` or `-1`. Although there is no separately named fixed-point theorem, sign reversal between the nonzero values ±1 implies that no tuple can equal its image. Thus the formal package also entails “with no fixed points,” with no added mathematical hypotheses.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.bab.justification: The signature quantifies over exactly the required lattice points, `∀ {A A' B B' : ℤ × ℤ}`, and assumes the four blueprint inequalities: `xCoord A' ≤ xCoord A`, `yCoord A ≤ yCoord A'`, `xCoord B' ≤ xCoord B`, and `yCoord B ≤ yCoord B'`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.bin.justification: The blueprint quantifies over “nonnegative integers” and assumes “a ≥ b and c ≥ d”; the Lean binders `∀ (a b c d : ℕ), b ≤ a → d ≤ c →` encode exactly those domains and inequalities. Its conclusion `↑(a.choose d) * ↑(b.choose c) ≤ ↑(a.choose c) * ↑(b.choose d)` is precisely `binom(a,d) binom(b,c) ≤ binom(a,c) binom(b,d)`. By the supplied docstring, `Nat.choose n k` is the binomial coefficient, including the zero cases, and the casts into `ℤ` preserve the intended integer-valued comparison. Thus the formal and informal statements agree.

The formal theorem quantifies over arbitrary sizes and natural-indexed data, `∀ {k : ℕ} (a b : Fin k → ℕ)`, and identifies `Matrix.of fun i j => ↑((a i).choose (b j))` with the stated path-weight matrix. Its dependencies instantiate exactly the blueprint data: `binomLatticeA a i = (0, -↑(a i))`, `binomLatticeB b i = (↑(b i), -↑(b i))`, and `unitArcWeight ... = 1`, on the integer lattice whose arcs are east or north steps. Moreover, `pathWeightMatrix` has entries `pathWeightSum ... (A i) (B j)`, so the right-hand side is precisely the matrix of unit-weight path sums. The use of `Fin k` merely encodes the blueprint’s finite index set, and the equality being written in the reverse order from “the path weight matrix equals the matrix” is immaterial by symmetry of equality.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.cat.justification: The target quantifies over exactly the required size, `∀ (k : ℕ)`, and asserts the stated matrix equality. Expanding `LGV.catalanHankelMatrix`, its `(i,j)` entry is `↑(catalan (↑i + ↑j))` for `i,j : Fin k`, matching “$(c_{i+j})_{0 \le i,j < k}$” (with the natural Catalan count cast into `ℤ`). Expanding `LGV.pathWeightMatrix`, the other entry is `LGV.pathWeightSum ... (fun i => (-(2 * ↑↑i), 0)) i (fun j => (2 * ↑↑j, 0)) j`, exactly using the specified vertices `A_i = (-2i,0)` and `B_j = (2j,0)`. The dependency `LGV.dyckDigraph` has up-right and down-right arcs with nonnegative height, and `LGV.dyckUnitArcWeight` is constantly `1`, so the path-weight sum is the integer count of Dyck paths, including the zero-arc path when the endpoints coincide. The path-finiteness and decidable-equality arguments are only infrastructure needed to form the finite path sums and add no mathematical restriction.

The blueprint quantifies over path tuples “in the Dyck digraph,” but the package contains no INFORMAL DEFINITION fixing that digraph’s vertex set and arc relation. The formal dependency makes a substantive choice: `LGV.dyckDigraph` has vertices `ℤ × ℕ` and arcs that move `(x,y)` to `(x+1,y+1)` or `(x+1,y-1)` while staying nonnegative. The only supplied informal graph definition, `def.lgv.lattice`, instead has vertices `ℤ²` and east/north arcs, so it cannot determine the meaning of “Dyck digraph” and is incompatible with paths that go “back down.” Thus it is unknown whether the formal graph is the graph intended by the blueprint. The indexing itself is compatible after translating the informal one-based `A_i := (-2(i-1),0)` to Lean’s zero-based binder `i : Fin k`, yielding the formal `A i = (-2 * ↑↑i, 0)`. To decide faithfulness, the package needs an informal definition of the Dyck digraph, or an explicit statement that it is the graph represented by `LGV.dyckDigraph`.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.coo.justification: The target quantifies without extra hypotheses over exactly “any lattice path p starting at A”: `∀ (path : LGV1.LatticePath) (start : LGV1.LatticePoint)`. Its conclusion, `(path.endpoint start).coordSum = start.coordSum + ↑path.stepCount`, matches `cs(endpoint(p,A)) = cs(A) + ℓ(p)`. The dependency bodies realize the informal meanings: `LatticePoint = ℤ × ℤ`, `coordSum p = p.1 + p.2`, `stepCount path = List.length path`, and `endpoint` folds the path’s east/north steps from the starting point. The cast `↑path.stepCount` merely embeds the natural-number length into ℤ so it can be added to the integer coordinate sum; it adds no mathematical restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.det.justification: The formal left-hand side is the determinant of the weighted path matrix: `LGV.pathWeightMatrix hpf w A B`, whose definition has entries `LGV.pathWeightSum hpf w (A i) (B j)`, i.e. sums of path weights. By contrast, the supplied informal definition fixes `M` as “the path count matrix ... with entries M_{i,j} = # paths(A_i → B_j)”, independent of `w`. Thus the formal identity is a weighted determinant identity, while the blueprint as defined equates the determinant of an unweighted count matrix with a generally weight-dependent sum `∑ (-1)^σ w(p)`. The discrepancy enters through the body of `LGV.pathWeightMatrix`, not through the summation over tuples. To make the declaration faithful, either the informal definition of `M` must be changed to the matrix whose `(i,j)` entry is the sum of weights of paths from `A_i` to `B_j`, or the formal statement must use a path-count matrix and correspondingly specialize `w` to unit weights (with an appropriate coefficient ring/cast). The binder `[DecidableEq V]` is only an encoding requirement for the path and finset definitions and is not the source of drift.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.dis.justification: The elaborated signature exactly matches the blueprint: `a ≤ b` fixes the interval ordering; `∀ (f : ℤ → ℤ), (∀ (n : ℤ), a ≤ n → n < b → |f (n + 1) - f n| ≤ 1)` expresses the step bound for every integer `n ∈ [a,b)`; `0 ≤ f a` and `f b ≤ 0` express `f(a) ≥ 0` and `f(b) ≤ 0`; and `∃ c, a ≤ c ∧ c ≤ b ∧ f c = 0` is exactly the existence of `c ∈ [a,b]` with `f(c)=0`. The explicit hypothesis `a ≤ b` is inherent in the blueprint’s use of endpoints `[a,b)` and `[a,b]`, and introduces no substantive mismatch.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.dyc.justification: The target asserts exactly `LGV.dyckDigraph.IsAcyclic`. The dependency `LGV.dyckDigraph` has vertex set `ℤ × ℕ` and arc relation `v.1 = u.1 + 1 ∧ v.2 = u.2 + 1 ∨ v.1 = u.1 + 1 ∧ v.2 + 1 = u.2 ∧ 0 < u.2`, matching the blueprint’s up-right and down-right arcs, with the down-step restricted to positive height. `LGV.SimpleDigraph.IsAcyclic` requires every path with `p.start = p.finish` to have `p.vertices.length = 1`; since paths are nonempty lists whose consecutive vertices are arcs, this says every closed directed path has zero arcs, faithfully expressing that the Dyck digraph is acyclic. There are no added binders or hypotheses.

The blueprint asserts “There is a bijection between paths from `(0, 0)` to `(2n, 0)` … and Dyck words of semilength `n`,” including fixed-`n` endpoint/length restrictions and inverse laws. The targets only define two conversions: `LGV.dyckWordToPath : DyckWord → LGV.dyckDigraph.Path` and `LGV.dyckPathToWord : (p : LGV.dyckDigraph.Path) → p.start = (0, 0) → p.finish.2 = 0 → DyckWord`. Neither declaration states that the conversions are mutually inverse, and neither is indexed or restricted by a fixed `n`; notably `dyckPathToWord` assumes only `p.finish.2 = 0`, not `p.finish = (2n, 0)`. Thus these constructions alone do not imply a bijection for each `n`. To make the formalization faithful, add a theorem or `Equiv` between paths satisfying `start = (0,0)` and `finish = (2n,0)` and Dyck words whose length is `2n` (or semilength is `n`), using these functions and proving both inverse identities.

The informal statement only says “Dyck digraph is path-finite” and provides no definition of “Dyck digraph.” The supplied informal definition `def.catalan.dyck` defines a “Dyck word,” while `def.lgv.lattice` defines the different integer-lattice digraph on `ℤ²`; neither fixes the graph meant here. The formal target asserts `LGV.dyckDigraph.IsPathFinite`, where `LGV.dyckDigraph` has vertices `ℤ × ℕ` and diagonal up/down arcs. Thus the path-finiteness predicate itself matches the phrase “path-finite,” via `∀ (u v), {p | p.start = u ∧ p.finish = v}.Finite`, but the package does not determine whether the formal graph is the blueprint’s intended Dyck digraph. An informal definition of the Dyck digraph—its vertex set and arcs—is needed; if it specifies `ℤ × ℕ` with the displayed up-right/down-right arcs, the declaration is faithful.

The formal binder `∀ (n : ℕ)` and equality `(LGV.pathsFromTo ... (0, 0) (2 * ↑n, 0)).card = catalan n` directly express the blueprint’s “number of paths from $(0,0)$ to $(2n,0)$ in the Dyck digraph equals the Catalan number $c_n$.” By the body of `LGV.dyckDigraph`, every arc increases the first coordinate by one and changes the natural-valued second coordinate by one up or down, so its paths are precisely lattice paths staying at nonnegative height. `pathsFromTo` is the finite set of paths with the specified endpoints, and `.card` counts them. The coercion `↑n : ℤ` merely encodes that the digraph’s first coordinate is integral. Finally, base-library `catalan n` denotes the recursive Catalan sequence, mathematically equivalent to the blueprint definition $c_n=\frac1{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$. No additional mathematical hypothesis or narrowed range is present.

The informal claim is “The number of paths from $(-2i,0)$ to $(2j,0)$ in the Dyck digraph equals $c_{i+j}$.” The target quantifies exactly over natural indices, `∀ (i j : ℕ)`, counts `(LGV.pathsFromTo LGV.dyckDigraph ... (-(2 * ↑i), 0) (2 * ↑j, 0)).card`, and equates this with `catalan (i + j)`. The dependency `LGV.dyckDigraph` has vertices `ℤ × ℕ` and precisely the up-right and permitted down-right arcs, so its paths are Dyck paths staying at nonnegative height. `pathsFromTo` is the finite set of all paths with the specified start and finish, and `Finset.card` is their number. The library `catalan` denotes the Catalan-number sequence, matching the informal definition of `c_{i+j}`; using its recursive implementation rather than the equivalent binomial formula does not change the stated number. There are no added mathematical hypotheses or narrowed ranges beyond the natural indexing implicit in the Catalan notation and endpoints.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.end.justification: The formal theorem quantifies exactly over “two lattice paths and A a starting point” via `∀ (path1 path2 : LGV1.LatticePath) (start : LGV1.LatticePoint)`. The dependencies give `LatticePath = List LatticeStep`, `LatticePoint = ℤ × ℤ`, and steps `east` and `north` with precisely the movements specified by `def.lgv.lattice`. List append in `(path1 ++ path2)` is therefore path concatenation, while `endpoint` is the left fold applying the steps in sequence. Thus `(path1 ++ path2).endpoint start = path2.endpoint (path1.endpoint start)` is exactly the displayed endpoint-of-concatenation identity, with no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

The target quantifies over every path and starting lattice point, `∀ (path : LGV1.LatticePath) (start : LGV1.LatticePoint)`, and concludes exactly `(path.endpoint start).1 = start.1 + ↑path.eastStepCount`. This matches the blueprint’s “The x-coordinate of the endpoint of a path p starting at A” and “x(A) + (# of east-steps in p).” The dependencies preserve the intended meanings: `LatticePoint = ℤ × ℤ`; `endpoint` folds the path’s steps from the start; `east` changes `(i,j)` to `(i+1,j)` while `north` leaves the first coordinate unchanged; and `eastStepCount` counts occurrences of `east`. The cast `↑path.eastStepCount` merely embeds the natural-number count into ℤ so it can be added to `start.1`, and introduces no substantive restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.exc.justification: The blueprint assumes “an acyclic digraph” and paths “sharing a vertex v”; the target has exactly `D.IsAcyclic → ∀ (p q : D.Path) (v : V) (hv_p : v ∈ p.vertices) (hv_q : v ∈ q.vertices)`. It defines `p'` and `q'` as the two components of `LGV.exchangeTails p q v hv_p hv_q`, then concludes that exchanging at `v` again gives `(p, q)`, exactly matching “exchanging the tails of p′ and q′ at v returns (p, q).” The `[DecidableEq V]` binder supports the computational definition of `Path.splitAt`, which uses `List.findIdx` and equality testing; it is an encoding requirement rather than an additional graph-theoretic hypothesis.

The formal conclusion exactly states the claimed weight preservation: `pathWeight w p * pathWeight w q = pathWeight w (...).1 * pathWeight w (...).2`, where `exchangeTails` is defined as `(head_p.concat tail_q ..., head_q.concat tail_p ...)`, matching the informal `(p', q')`. The informal hypothesis that `D` is “an acyclic digraph” is omitted: the signature quantifies over every `{D : LGV.SimpleDigraph V}`. This is a valid strengthening/generalization, since it includes all acyclic simple digraphs and the identity does not require acyclicity. Likewise, repeated occurrences of `v` only arise in the extra generality; on an acyclic path the occurrence is unique, while `splitAt` selects the first occurrence in general. The binder `[DecidableEq V]` is an implementation-level requirement used by `splitAt` through `List.findIdx`, rather than a substantive restriction on the combinatorial claim. Finally, `[CommRing K]` supplies the commutative multiplication needed to reorder the four path-segment weights; the theorem is polymorphic over all such weight rings rather than being restricted to the particular lattice weights from the surrounding context.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.fir.justification: The informal statement assumes “an intersecting signed path tuple” and the formal declarations likewise take `(spt : LGV1.SignedPathTuple2 A A' B B')` and `h : spt.isIntersecting`. By definition, `spt.isIntersecting` is `∃ v ∈ spt.path0.vertices A, v ∈ spt.path1.vertices A'`, exactly expressing that the two paths share a vertex. `LGV1.firstIntersectionIdx` is `List.findIdx (fun v => decide (v ∈ verts1)) verts0`, where `verts0 = spt.path0.vertices A` and `verts1 = spt.path1.vertices A'`; `List.findIdx` returns the index of the first satisfying element, so this is the smallest index whose path0 vertex belongs to path1’s vertices. Finally, `firstIntersectionIdx_lt` concludes `LGV1.firstIntersectionIdx spt h < (spt.path0.vertices A).length`, exactly the claimed strict bound by the number of vertices of `p₀`. The definition of `LatticePath.vertices` yields the visited vertices including the start and end, as required.

The blueprint unconditionally says that after applying the involution, “the first intersection point of the resulting path tuple is still v,” which in particular asserts that the resulting tuple is intersecting. The Lean target instead adds the binder `(h' : (LGV1.ipatInvolution spt h).isIntersecting)` and proves the equality only under that assumption. This is a mathematically substantive added hypothesis, not merely a decidability or ambient-setting instance: `isIntersecting` means `∃ v ∈ path0.vertices A, v ∈ path1.vertices A'`. The formal declarations collectively match all three blueprint properties for every intersecting signed path tuple, with exactly the blueprint hypothesis `(h : spt.isIntersecting)`. The point is defined by `firstIntersection spt h = (spt.path0.vertices A)[firstIntersectionIdx spt h]`, and `firstIntersection_mem_path0` proves it lies in `spt.path0.vertices A`, matching “v lies on p₀ (at the first intersection index).” `firstIntersection_mem_path1` proves `firstIntersection spt h ∈ spt.path1.vertices A'`, matching “v lies on p₁.” Finally, `firstIntersection_is_first` proves `∀ (i : ℕ) (hi : i < idx), (spt.path0.vertices A)[i] ∉ spt.path1.vertices A'`, exactly matching “no vertex of p₀ at an earlier index belongs to p₁.” The dependency `firstIntersectionIdx` uses `List.findIdx` on membership in path1, whose documented meaning is the first satisfying index, and `h` ensures such an index exists.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.ipa.justification: Both declarations exactly formalize the two clauses of the blueprint. The first target states `∀ {k} {A B} (pt : PathTuple k A B), pt.isIntersecting ↔ ∃ v, pt.isCrowded v`, matching “a path tuple is intersecting if and only if it has at least one crowded vertex.” Here `isIntersecting` is `¬ pt.isNonIntersecting`, exactly the informal definition, while `isCrowded v` is `∃ i j, i ≠ j ∧ v ∈ pt.verticesOf i ∧ v ∈ pt.verticesOf j`, exactly requiring that the vertex lie on two distinct paths. The second target states `pt.isIntersecting ↔ pt.crowdedPathIndices.Nonempty`, matching the equivalent claim that “its set of crowded path indices is nonempty.” The dependency defines those indices as `{i | ∃ j, i ≠ j ∧ ¬Disjoint (pt.verticesOf i) (pt.verticesOf j)}`, i.e. indices whose path shares a vertex with another distinct path. The binders quantify over every natural `k`, endpoints `A B`, and path tuple `pt`, with no additional mathematically substantive hypotheses.

The target states exactly `∀ {k : ℕ} (A B : LGV1.kVertex k), (LGV1.ipatsFromTo A B).Finite`, matching “For any two k-vertices A, B, the set of ipats from A to B is finite.” The dependency `kVertex k = Fin k → LatticePoint` represents a k-tuple of lattice points, while `PathTuple k A B` consists of k indexed lattice paths satisfying `isPathFromTo (A i) (B i)`. Finally, `ipatsFromTo A B = {pt | pt.isIntersecting}` and `isIntersecting pt = ¬ pt.isNonIntersecting`, matching the informal definition of an ipat as a path tuple that is not non-intersecting. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.lat.justification: The target quantifies over every starting point via `(start : ℤ × ℤ)` and gives an equivalence `LGV.LatticePath' ≃ { p // p.start = start }`. The target states for every `∀ {k : ℕ} {A B : LGV.kVertex (ℤ × ℤ) k} (pt : LGV.LatticePath'Tuple k A B)` that `pt.isIntersecting ↔ (LGV.latticePath'TupleToPathTuple pt).isIntersecting`, exactly matching “A step-based lattice path tuple is intersecting if and only if the corresponding vertex-based path tuple is intersecting.” The conversion uses `(pt.paths i).toPath (A i)`, whose vertex list is `toVertices`, while the step-based predicate uses `verticesOf i := {p | p ∈ (pt.paths i).toVertices (A i)}`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.mon.justification: The blueprint says: “If σ ∈ S_k satisfies σ(i) ≤ σ(j) whenever i < j, then σ = id.” The elaborated signature quantifies over exactly a permutation of the k-element set, `∀ {k : ℕ} (σ : Equiv.Perm (Fin k))`, assumes exactly `(∀ (i j : Fin k), i < j → σ i ≤ σ j)`, and concludes `σ = Equiv.refl (Fin k)`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.nes.justification: The formal construction matches every component of the blueprint. The binder `ℕ → LGV.dyckDigraph.Path` corresponds to “For each i ∈ ℕ” and makes `γ_i` a path in the Dyck digraph. Its vertices are exactly `List.finRange (4 * n + 1)` mapped to `(↑i - 2 * ↑n, min i (4 * n - i))`, which is the stated sequence `(j - 2i, min (j, 4i - j))` for `j = 0, …, 4i`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.nip.justification: The target quantifies exactly over all natural numbers and all pairs of k-vertices: `∀ {k : ℕ} (A B : LGV1.kVertex k)`, matching “For any two k-vertices A, B.” Its conclusion `(LGV1.nipatsFromTo A B).Finite` directly states that the corresponding set is finite. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.lgv.pat.justification: The blueprint says: “If path $h$ goes from $A$ to $v$ and path $t$ goes from $v$ to $B$, then $h \cdot t$ goes from $A$ to $B$.” The target quantifies exactly over paths and points, `∀ (head tail : LGV1.LatticePath) (A v B : LGV1.LatticePoint)`, and asserts `head.isPathFromTo A v → tail.isPathFromTo v B → (head ++ tail).isPathFromTo A B`. (w : LGV.ArcWeight D K)`. Its summand `↑↑(Equiv.Perm.sign sp.fst) * LGV.pathTupleWeight w sp.snd.paths` is exactly the permutation sign `(-1)^σ` times the tuple weight. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.linalg..justification: The formal binders `{F : Type u_1} [Field F] {V : Type u_2} [AddCommGroup V] [Module F V] {k : ℕ} (v : Fin k → V)` faithfully encode a field, an F-vector space, and a k-tuple. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.mem_cyc.justification: The blueprint’s domain includes 1-cycles: Definition `def.perm.cycs.cycs` explicitly says “This includes $1$-cycles,” while the target requires `(hc : c.IsCycle)`, whose supplied docstring defines a cycle as “a non-identity permutation.” Thus the formal binder excludes the blueprint’s 1-cycles. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.mem_sam.justification: The binders match the blueprint: `[Fintype α]` formalizes “Let X be a finite set,” `σ : Equiv.Perm α` is a permutation, `i j : α` gives `i, j ∈ X`, and `i ∈ σ.support` is exactly “i not a fixed point of σ,” since `support` is documented as the finset of nonfixed points. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.minor.e.justification: The blueprint states “The minor of the empty sets is 1: det (sub_∅^∅ A) = 1.” The target universally quantifies over a commutative ring, dimensions, and matrix—“∀ {R} [CommRing R] {n m} (A : Matrix (Fin n) (Fin m) R)”—and concludes “minor A ∅ ∅ = 1.” By the body of `minor`, since the two empty finsets have equal cardinality, `minor A ∅ ∅` is exactly the determinant of `A.submatrix` along their canonical increasing embeddings, i.e. the 0×0 matrix `sub_∅^∅ A`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.module..justification: The blueprint states: “Let K be a commutative ring and M a K-module. For any a,b∈M, we have −(a+b)=(−a)+(−b).” The formal declaration proves exactly the same equality, `∀ {M : Type u_2} [AddCommGroup M] (a b : M), -(a + b) = -a + -b`. The blueprint says: “Let K be a commutative ring and M a K-module. For any a∈M, we have -(-a)=a.” Its module axioms make the additive structure on M a commutative group, with negation given by the additive inverse. The blueprint quantifies over “a commutative ring” K, “a K-module” M, and “any a,b∈M”; the elaborated signature matches this with `∀ {K : Type u_1} [CommRing K] {M : Type u_2} [AddCommGroup M] [Module K M] (a b : M)`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.multipl.justification: The blueprint quantifies only “Under the same assumptions as Lemma \ref{lem.summable-fiber-discrete},” but the package does not include that lemma’s statement. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.neg_one.justification: The blueprint states: “In any integral domain where $-1 \neq 1$, the element $-1$ is a primitive $2$nd root of unity.” The elaborated signature assumes only `∀ {K : Type u_1} [CommRing K], -1 ≠ 1 → IsPrimitiveRoot (-1) 2`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.nonbloc.justification: The binders match the blueprint exactly: `∀ {K : Type u_1} [Field K] {ω : K} {d : ℕ}, IsPrimitiveRoot ω d → 1 < d → ∀ (n k : ℕ), ...` formalizes “Let K be a field, d ≥ 2, and ω a primitive d-th root of unity. For n,k ∈ ℕ.” For natural `d`, `1 < d` is precisely `d ≥ 2`. Under this hypothesis, the library definition of `IsPrimitiveRoot ω d`—`ω ^ d = 1` and every exponent `l` with `ω ^ l = 1` is divisible by `d`—is equivalent to the informal definition excluding roots at exponents `1,…,d−1`. The summation domain is also exact: `kSubsets n k` has body `Finset.powersetCard k (Finset.range n)`, and filtering by `¬ IsDBlocky d n S` gives exactly the non-d-blocky k-element subsets of `[n]`. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.num_tra.justification: The blueprint states: “The number of transpositions in $S_X$ (for a finite set $X$) is $\binom{|X|}{2}$.” The formal binders `∀ (X : Type u_1) [DecidableEq X] [Fintype X]` encode a finite set/type, while `Equiv.Perm X` is precisely the type of bijections from `X` to itself, hence $S_X$. The `DecidableEq X` instance is computational infrastructure needed by `IsSwap` and finite-set membership, not an additional mathematical restriction on finite sets.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.numcycl.justification: The blueprint says the total is “the number of nontrivial cycles … plus the number of fixed points.” The body is exactly `σ.cycleFactorsFinset.card + (Fintype.card α - σ.support.card)`: `cycleFactorsFinset.card` counts the nontrivial cycle factors, while `support` is documented as the finset of nonfixed points, so `Fintype.card α - σ.support.card` counts the fixed points. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.ca.justification: The formal binders exactly encode the blueprint hypotheses: `∀ (I : Set ℕ) ... (∀ i ∈ I, i > 0)` expresses `I ⊆ {1,2,3,…}`, while `∀ (n d j : ℕ), d ∈ I → d * j ≤ n →` matches “let `d ∈ I`, and let `d · j ≤ n`.” The conclusion filters `Nat.Partition.restricted n (fun x => x ∈ I)` by `Multiset.count d p.parts ≥ j`, takes its `Finset.card`, and equates it with the card of `restricted (n - d * j) I`, exactly matching the stated cardinality identity. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.co.justification: The target quantifies exactly over natural exponents, `∀ (n : ℕ)`, as required by the coefficient definition, which says “If `n ∈ ℕ`” then `[x^n]a := a_n`. Its left side, `(PowerSeries.coeff n) Nat.Partition.P`, is therefore precisely `[x^n]P`. The right side `↑(Nat.Partition.partitionCount n)` is that count cast into ℤ, matching the coefficient ring, since `partitionCount n = Fintype.card n.Partition` and `Nat.Partition` means partitions of n. Thus the formal equality expresses `[x^n]P = p(n)` for every relevant `n`.

The target quantifies exactly over natural indices, `∀ (n : ℕ)`, as required by the coefficient notation definition. Its left side, `(PowerSeries.coeff n) (Nat.Partition.S * Nat.Partition.P)`, is precisely `[x^n](S·P)`. On the right, `∑ k ∈ Finset.range n, divisorSum (k + 1) * partitionCount (n - k - 1)` ranges over `k = 0,…,n-1`; reindexing by `j = k+1` gives exactly `∑_{j=1}^n σ(j)·p(n-j)`. The outer cast merely places this natural-number sum in the integer coefficient ring `ℤ`, matching `S,P ∈ ℤ[[x]]`. For `n=0`, both formulations use the empty sum.

Here `PowerSeries.coeff` is documented as the nth coefficient, `PowerSeries.X` as the power-series variable, and `PowerSeries.derivative` as the formal derivative. The cast `↑n : ℤ` merely expresses multiplication by `n` in the coefficient ring `ℤ`. Finally, `Nat.Partition.P` is the integer partition generating function, matching the blueprint’s `P := ∑_{n≥0} p(n)x^n`. There are no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

The elaborated signature states `∀ (n d : ℕ) (p : n.Partition), 0 < d → Multiset.count d p.parts ≤ n / d`, exactly matching “For any partition `p` of `n` and `d > 0`, `count(d,p) ≤ n/d`.” Here `Nat.Partition` is documented as a partition into positive integers summing to `n`, `p.parts` is its multiset of parts, `Multiset.count` is multiplicity, and natural-number division `/` rounds downward. The restriction `n : ℕ` is consistent with the available `Nat.Partition` representation and does not omit any possible partition of a negative integer, since a finite tuple of positive integers cannot have negative size.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.di.justification: The blueprint quantifies over “any function $f$” but gives neither its domain nor, decisively, its codomain. The arguments $f(n-k-1)$ suggest a natural-number domain, but the displayed sums and products could take values in ℕ, ℤ, or an ambient commutative ring. The target specifically restricts this to `(f : ℕ → ℕ)`. The supplied commutative-ring definitions do not resolve the ambiguity because the statement never binds a ring or says that `f` takes values in one. If the intended type is `ℕ → ℕ`, the declaration is faithful: `(I : Set ℕ)` is even slightly more general than a set of positive integers, since zero never occurs in `Nat.divisors (k+1)` or `Finset.Icc 1 n`, and `[DecidablePred fun x => x ∈ I]` is an implementation requirement for filtering. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.fi.justification: The formal hypothesis `i < Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts` exactly expresses “For i < largest part of p”: folding `max` over `p.parts` with initial value `0` gives its largest part and gives `0` for the empty partition, matching `largest-part-0`. The conclusion `0 < (Multiset.filter (fun x => x > i) p.parts).card` says that the multiset of parts greater than `i` has positive cardinality, which is equivalent to that collection being nonempty. The binder `p : n.Partition` supplies precisely a partition, whose `parts` are positive natural numbers summing to `n`; the implicit natural-number quantification over `i` is appropriate for comparison with those parts.

The target quantifies over every natural number and partition, `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition)`, and asserts `(Multiset.filter (fun x => x > 0) p.parts).card = p.parts.card`. By the supplied `Nat.Partition` and `Nat.Partition.parts` docstrings, a partition’s parts are positive natural numbers. By `Multiset.filter`, filtering with `x > 0` retains exactly those positive parts with their multiplicities, and `Multiset.card` is their cardinality. Thus this exactly formalizes that, for a partition `p`, keeping only its positive parts preserves cardinality because every part is already positive. Restricting the formal index to `n : ℕ` is consistent with `Nat.Partition`; although the general informal definition mentions partitions of integer `n`, the stated lemma itself merely says “For a partition `p`” and imposes no separate integer-index quantifier.

The formal declaration explicitly quantifies `∀ (n m : ℕ)`, while the informal statement merely says “partitions of $n$ whose largest part is $\le m$” and does not state the domains of `n` and `m`. This matters because `def.pars.parts` defines “a partition of $n$” for `n \in \mathbb Z`, whereas the target only covers natural-number indices; moreover, allowing a negative `m` would make the claimed equivalence fail for the empty partition, whose largest part is defined as `0` although “all parts ≤ m” is vacuous. If the missing ambient convention is `n,m \in \mathbb N`, the target is faithful: `largestPart` is `Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, matching the empty-partition convention, and `Nat.Partition.restricted n (fun x => x ≤ m)` means every part is at most `m`. The package needs the blueprint’s ambient binder/domain convention for `n` and `m` to decide whether the natural-number binders are faithful or a restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.is.justification: The target states `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition), p.IsDistinctParts ↔ p.parts.Nodup`, exactly matching “A partition is into distinct parts iff its parts multiset has no duplicates.” The dependency defines `p.IsDistinctParts` by `p.parts.Nodup`, while `Multiset.Nodup` means every part has multiplicity at most one, which is precisely that the parts are distinct. Quantifying over `n : ℕ` is appropriate because a finite partition into positive integers necessarily has a nonnegative size; thus it does not omit any partitions described by the informal definitions.

The target states `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition), p.IsDistinctParts ↔ ∀ (i : ℕ), Multiset.count i p.parts ≤ 1`, exactly matching “A partition is into distinct parts iff each part appears at most once.” The dependency defines `p.IsDistinctParts` as `p.parts.Nodup`, and `Multiset.Nodup` means precisely that every element has multiplicity at most 1. Quantifying over every `i : ℕ`, rather than only over values occurring as parts, does not strengthen the condition materially, since absent values have count zero. Using `n : ℕ` is faithful to the represented setting: partitions have positive integer parts, hence nonnegative size; negative integers admit no such partitions.

The informal statement says, “A partition is into odd parts iff all its parts are odd.” The target states exactly `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition), p.IsOddParts ↔ ∀ i ∈ p.parts, Odd i`. Moreover, the dependency `Nat.Partition.IsOddParts` is defined by `fun {n} p => ∀ i ∈ p.parts, Odd i`, matching informal Definition (a): a partition into odd parts is one “whose all parts are odd.” Thus both sides of the equivalence coincide definitionally. Restricting the index to `n : ℕ` is inherent in the available `Nat.Partition : ℕ → Type`; it introduces no additional hypothesis on represented partitions.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.iv.justification: The blueprint states “[P ∧ Q] = [P] · [Q]”, with `[A]` equal to `1` when `A` is true and `0` otherwise. The project definition is exactly `if P then 1 else 0`, and the target concludes `IversonBracket.iverson (P ∧ Q) = IversonBracket.iverson P * IversonBracket.iverson Q`. The binder `{α : Type u_1} [MulZeroOneClass α]` generalizes the blueprint’s integer-valued bracket to every type having the required multiplication, zero, and one structure; this is a stronger, more general statement and includes the integer case. The binders `[Decidable P] [Decidable Q]` merely provide the decision procedures required to form the `if` expressions (and induce decidability of `P ∧ Q`), so they encode the formal setting rather than add a mathematically substantive restriction.

The dependency defines `IversonBracket.iverson P` exactly as `if P then 1 else 0`, matching the informal truth value “1 if true; 0 if false.” The target states `IversonBracket.iverson P = 1 ↔ P`. Its binders `[Zero α] [One α] [NeZero 1]` generalize the informal integer-valued bracket to any type whose `1` is nonzero; `[NeZero 1]` ensures that the false branch `0` cannot equal `1`. This does not weaken the intended integer statement, but makes the theorem strictly more general. The binder `[Decidable P]` is only the formal encoding needed by the `if P then ... else ...` definition.

The formal conclusion `IversonBracket.iverson P = 0 ↔ ¬P` exactly matches “The Iverson bracket equals 0 iff the proposition is false.” By definition, `iverson P` is `if P then 1 else 0`, matching the informal truth value. The binder `[NeZero 1]` encodes the stated assumption “assuming 1 ≠ 0,” as fixed by the `NeZero` docstring. The binders `[Decidable P]` and the zero/one structures are needed to form the conditional and its values; quantifying over arbitrary `{α}` with `[Zero α] [One α]` is strictly more general than the informal integer-valued formulation, not a weakening. Thus the Lean theorem implies the blueprint statement.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.la.justification: The target quantifies over exactly “a partition of n” via `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition)` and concludes `p.largestPart ≤ n`, matching “the largest part is at most n.” The dependency defines `p.largestPart` as `Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, which is the maximum of the parts and gives `0` for the empty partition, exactly matching convention `conv.pars.largest-part-0`. Although the informal partition definition permits `n ∈ ℤ` while Lean indexes partitions by `n : ℕ`, a finite tuple of positive integers cannot have negative size, so no negative-index case is omitted; the restriction is not mathematically contentful.

The formal statement `∀ {n m : ℕ} (p : n.Partition), p.largestPart ≤ m ↔ ∀ i ∈ p.parts, i ≤ m` exactly matches “A partition has largest part ≤ m if and only if all its parts are ≤ m.” Here `p.parts` is the multiset of the partition’s positive-integer parts, and `largestPart` is defined as `Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, i.e. their maximum. Its value on the empty partition is `0`, exactly as required by `conv.pars.largest-part-0`. The binders over `n`, `m`, and `p : n.Partition` add no contentful restriction: `Nat.Partition` represents partitions of natural-number size, while a partition into positive integers necessarily has nonnegative size.

The elaborated signature exactly states “For $n>0$, every partition of $n$ has a positive largest part”: `∀ {n : ℕ}, n > 0 → ∀ (p : n.Partition), 0 < p.largestPart`. Here `{n : ℕ}` and `n > 0` match “For $n>0$,” `∀ (p : n.Partition)` matches “every partition of $n$,” and `0 < p.largestPart` matches “has a positive largest part.” The dependency `largestPart` is `Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, which computes the maximum part and gives the empty partition value `0`, exactly matching `conv.pars.largest-part-0`. Restricting `n` to `ℕ` does not lose any positive integer cases, since a partition of a positive integer has a natural-number size.

The target quantifies over exactly the relevant objects, `∀ (p : Nat.Partition 0)`, and concludes `p.largestPart = 0`, matching “The largest part of the partition of 0 is 0.” The dependency defines `largestPart` as `Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, so its value on the empty partition is 0, exactly implementing the convention “the largest part of the empty partition … is 0.” Finally, `Nat.Partition` consists of multisets of positive integers summing to the index, so a partition indexed by 0 has no positive parts and corresponds to the unique empty partition. No additional mathematically contentful hypotheses or restrictions are present.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.lh.justification: The formal equality matches the blueprint term-for-term: `n * (Nat.Partition.restricted n fun x => x ∈ I).card` formalizes `n·|restricted(n,I)|`, while `∑ p ∈ Nat.Partition.restricted n fun x => x ∈ I, p.parts.sum` sums the parts of each restricted partition, corresponding to `∑_{p∈restricted(n,I)} |p|`. By the library definitions, `restricted` consists exactly of partitions whose every part satisfies membership in `I`, and `p.parts.sum` is the sum (size) of the partition. The formal quantifier `∀ (I : Set ℕ)` is slightly more general than the blueprint’s `I ⊆ {1,2,3,…}`; this does not weaken the theorem, and membership of `0` is immaterial because partition parts are positive. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.nu.justification: The target quantifies `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition)` and concludes `p.numParts ≤ n`. By the dependency body, `p.numParts` is `p.parts.card`, exactly the number/length of the partition’s parts, while `Nat.Partition` is documented as a multiset of positive integers summing to `n`. Thus the conclusion is precisely that the number of positive summands is at most their sum. Although the informal definition allows the phrase “partition of n” for `n ∈ ℤ`, every finite tuple of positive integers has nonnegative size, so no partition of a negative integer exists; indexing the realizable cases by `n : ℕ` is therefore an encoding choice rather than a mathematically contentful restriction.

The formal binders `∀ {n : ℕ}, n > 0 → ∀ (p : n.Partition)` exactly match “For $n>0$, every partition of $n$.” Its conclusion `0 < p.numParts` says that the number of parts is positive, hence that the partition “has at least one part.” This meaning is fixed by `Nat.Partition.numParts`, whose body is `p.parts.card`; `Multiset.card` is the cardinality/length of the parts multiset. Thus `0 < p.numParts` is precisely the assertion that there is at least one part. The use of `n : ℕ` is consistent with the statement’s explicit `$n>0$` and does not introduce a contentful restriction, since a positive integer is natural.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.pa.justification: The blueprint says every partition of n “into 2 parts” has the form `{n-b, b}` for some `1 ≤ b ≤ ⌊n/2⌋`. The formal hypothesis `p.parts.card = 2` expresses two parts, while the conclusion `∃ b, 1 ≤ b ∧ 2 * b ≤ n ∧ p.parts = {n - b, b}` gives exactly that multiset form. For natural numbers, `2 * b ≤ n` is equivalent to `b ≤ ⌊n/2⌋`. Using `Nat.Partition` is faithful: its documented meaning is a multiset of positive integers summing to `n`; although the informal definition allows an integer index `n`, any integer admitting a partition is necessarily nonnegative, so negative indices add only vacuous cases.

The formal signature `∀ (n : ℕ), 0 < Nat.Partition.partitionCount n` exactly matches “For every $n\in\mathbb N$, we have $p(n)>0$.” By definition, `Nat.Partition.partitionCount n = Fintype.card n.Partition`, and `Nat.Partition` is documented as partitions of `n`—multisets of positive integers summing to `n`—which represents the informal weakly decreasing tuples of positive integers. Thus the formal theorem says that the number of partitions of every natural number, including zero, is positive, with no added hypotheses or narrowed quantifiers.

The blueprint says, “The length of the partition of $0$ is $0$.” Its definitions make a partition a finite tuple of positive integers and its length the number of entries. The Lean theorem quantifies over every partition of zero, `∀ (p : Nat.Partition 0)`, and concludes `p.parts.card = 0`. Here `Nat.Partition.parts` is the multiset of positive parts and `Multiset.card` is its length, so this exactly states that every partition of 0 has length 0.

The target quantifies `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition), ∀ i ∈ p.parts, i ≤ n`, exactly asserting that every entry `i` among the parts of a partition of `n` is at most `n`. This matches “A partition of $n$ has all parts $\leq n$.” The base-library meanings support the blueprint definitions: `Nat.Partition` is “a multiset of positive integers summing to `n`,” and `Nat.Partition.parts` returns those positive integers. Although the informal definition indexes partitions by `n ∈ ℤ` while Lean uses `n : ℕ`, this does not omit any actual integer partitions: a finite sum of positive integers is nonnegative, so no partition of a negative integer exists. Thus the natural-number indexing captures every nonvacuous case.

The blueprint says, “The partition of $0$ has no parts (i.e., it is the empty tuple).” The Lean signature quantifies over every such partition, `∀ (p : Nat.Partition 0)`, and concludes `p.parts = 0`. Here `Nat.Partition.parts` is the multiset of positive integer parts, while `0 : Multiset ℕ` is the zero/empty multiset via `Multiset.instZero`. Thus the conclusion says exactly that every partition of 0 has an empty collection of parts, with no added hypotheses or restricted quantifiers.

The target quantifies only `∀ (k n : ℕ)`, whereas the blueprint definition of the notation states: “Let `n ∈ ℤ` and `k ∈ ℕ`. Then, we set `p_k(n) := ...`.” Thus the target narrows the blueprint’s integer quantifier on `n` to nonnegative integers. This restriction enters through `Nat.Partition.partsCount : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`, specifically its second argument, and is propagated to the target binder `n : ℕ`. To make the formalization faithful, define or extend the partition-count function to accept `n : ℤ`—with count zero for negative `n`—and state the equivalence for `∀ (k : ℕ) (n : ℤ)`, interpreting comparisons with `k` in `ℤ`.

The blueprint definition fixes the domain as “Let n∈ℤ and k∈ℕ” for p_k(n), while the target quantifies only “∀ {k n : ℕ}”. This is a mathematically contentful restriction excluding negative integers. Moreover, the restriction enters through the dependencies: `Nat.Partition.partsCount : ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`, `partsWithOne : ℕ → (n : ℕ) → Finset n.Partition`, and `partsWithoutOne` likewise, while `Nat.Partition : ℕ → Type` can only represent partitions indexed by natural sizes. Thus the full integer-indexed blueprint statement cannot be expressed with these definitions. To make it statable and faithful, the project would need integer-indexed versions or extensions of these counting functions and partition subsets—returning empty sets/count zero for negative `n`—after which the theorem should quantify `n : ℤ` and `k : ℕ`.

The blueprint notation is fixed by `def.pars.pn-pkn`: “Let `n ∈ ℤ` and `k ∈ ℕ`” and defines `p_k(n)` for every integer `n`. Thus the displayed identity ranges over integer `n` (with natural `k,m`). The target instead has the narrowed binder `∀ (n m : ℕ)`, and both referenced project definitions have type `ℕ → ℕ → ℕ`: `Nat.Partition.partsCount` and `Nat.Partition.partsLeqCount`. Hence the formal declaration only covers natural `n` and does not imply the blueprint statement for negative integers. Moreover, with the supplied project definitions, partitions and both counting functions are indexed only by `ℕ`, so the integer-domain statement cannot be stated directly. To make it faithful, the dependencies would need integer-indexed counting definitions (returning zero for negative sizes), followed by a target quantified as `n : ℤ, m : ℕ`; alternatively, the informal definition and statement would need to restrict `n` to `ℕ`.

The binders `∀ {k n : ℕ}, k > 0 → n > 0 →` exactly match “For $k>0$ and $n>0$.” By definition, `Nat.Partition.partsWithOne k n = {p | p.parts.card = k ∧ p.containsOne}`, and `containsOne` means `1 ∈ p.parts`, so its cardinality is precisely the number of partitions of `n` into `k` parts containing 1. Also, `Nat.Partition.partsCount (k - 1) (n - 1)` is the number of partitions of `n-1` into exactly `k-1` parts, matching `$p_{k-1}(n-1)$`. The blueprint’s definition quantifies the size over integers: “Let n ∈ ℤ … p_k(n) := (# of partitions of n into k parts),” while the target restricts both indices to naturals: “∀ {k n : ℕ}.” This is a mathematically contentful narrowing, not merely encoding. stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.qb.justification: The blueprint assumes “Let F be a finite field” and “V be an n-dimensional F-vector space.” These are represented by `[Field F] [Fintype F]`, `[Module F V] [Module.Finite F V]`, and the hypothesis `Module.finrank F V = n`. Here `Module.Finite` is part of encoding finite-dimensionality, not an additional mathematical restriction. The conclusion `Nat.card { v // LinearIndependent F v } = ∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, (Fintype.card F ^ n - Fintype.card F ^ i)` counts the linearly independent families indexed by `Fin k`, i.e. k-tuples, and `Finset.range k` is exactly the index range `0 ≤ i < k`. Thus its right-hand side is precisely `∏_{i=0}^{k-1} (|F|^n - |F|^i)`. Natural-number subtraction is appropriate for cardinalities; when `k > n`, the factor at `i = n` is zero. The formal and informal statements therefore agree.

The blueprint states: “The number of weakly increasing k-tuples from {0,1,…,ℓ} equals binom(k+ℓ,k).” The target universally quantifies the same natural parameters, `∀ (k ℓ : ℕ)`, and asserts `(monotoneFunctions k ℓ).card = (k + ℓ).choose k`. By the dependency body, `monotoneFunctions k ℓ` is exactly `{f : Fin k → Fin (ℓ + 1) | Monotone f}`, and its docstring identifies these as weakly increasing `k`-tuples with entries in `{0,…,ℓ}`. `Finset.card` counts them, while `Nat.choose` is the natural-number binomial coefficient. There are no additional hypotheses or narrowed ranges.

The formal binders `∀ (k m s : ℕ), s ≤ k * m →` exactly encode “For each s ≤ k · m.” The filtered set `{f ∈ monotoneFunctions k m | ∑ i, ↑(f i) = s}` consists, by the dependency body `fun k m => {f | Monotone f}`, of weakly increasing functions `Fin k → Fin (m + 1)`, hence weakly increasing k-tuples with entries in `{0,1,…,m}`, restricted to value sum `s`. The right side uses `partitionsInBox s k m`, whose body requires `μ.parts.card ≤ k ∧ ∀ p ∈ μ.parts, p ≤ m`; since `μ : s.Partition`, these are exactly the partitions of `s` fitting in a `k × m` box. Equality of the two `Finset.card` values therefore states precisely the claimed equality of numbers.

The blueprint assumes “Let n, k ∈ ℕ with k ≤ n,” exactly matched by the target binders “(n k : ℕ), k ≤ n.” Its sum from m = 0 through k(n−k) is exactly represented by “m ∈ Finset.range (k * (n - k) + 1).” The dependency `partitionsInBox m k (n-k)` has body `{μ | μ.parts.card ≤ k ∧ ∀ p ∈ μ.parts, p ≤ n-k}`, which is precisely the set of partitions of size m fitting in a k × (n−k) box. Its cardinality acts by natural-number scalar multiplication in “card • q ^ m,” matching the coefficient times q^m. Finally, `qBinomial` sums q raised to the weights of weakly increasing k-tuples in `{0,…,n−k}`, the standard zero-padded/reversed encoding of partitions with length ≤ k and largest part ≤ n−k. The additional generality “∀ {R} [CommSemiring R] … ∀ (q : R)” strengthens the polynomial identity to all commutative-semiring evaluations; it does not weaken or distort the blueprint statement, which follows by taking the polynomial ring and its indeterminate.

The elaborated binders `∀ {R : Type u_2} [Field R] (n : ℕ) (q : R)` exactly encode “Over a field” with arbitrary `n` and `q`. The hypothesis `(∀ i ∈ Finset.range n, q ^ (i + 1) ≠ 1)` quantifies over `i = 0, …, n-1`, hence over exponents `i + 1 = 1, …, n`, exactly matching “if q^i ≠ 1 for all i = 1, …, n”. The conclusion `AlgebraicCombinatorics.qFactorial n q ≠ 0` matches `[n]_q! ≠ 0`, since `qFactorial` is defined as `∏ i ∈ Finset.range n, qInt (i + 1) q` and `qInt k q` as `∑ i ∈ Finset.range k, q ^ i`, agreeing with the informal definitions `[n]_q! = [1]_q⋯[n]_q` and `[k]_q = q^0+⋯+q^(k-1)`.

The target states, for all natural numbers `n k` with `k ≤ n`, that `qFactorial n q = (∏ i ∈ Finset.range k, qInt (n - i) q) * qFactorial (n - k) q`. Since `Finset.range k` consists of `0,…,k-1`, the product is exactly `[n]_q · [n-1]_q · … · [n-k+1]_q`, matching the blueprint. The dependency bodies also match the informal definitions: `qInt n q = ∑ i ∈ range n, q^i` and `qFactorial n q = ∏ i ∈ range n, qInt (i+1) q`. The binder `{R} [CommSemiring R] ... (q : R)` is strictly more general than the blueprint’s polynomial/commutative-ring setting: it permits arbitrary evaluations of `q` in any commutative semiring, while specializing to the stated setting yields the blueprint identity. This weaker algebraic assumption and wider quantification strengthen rather than weaken the theorem.

The target states `∀ {R : Type u_2} [CommRing R] (n : ℕ) (q : R), (1 - q) * qInt n q = 1 - q ^ n`, while `qInt` is exactly `∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, q ^ i`, i.e. `q⁰ + ⋯ + qⁿ⁻¹`. Thus it directly formalizes “For any n ∈ ℕ, (1-q)·[n]₍q₎ = 1-qⁿ.” Quantifying over every commutative ring and every element `q` is strictly more general than taking the polynomial/FPS indeterminate and is licensed by informal Definition (c), which defines `[n]ₐ` by substitution in any ring. The displayed quotient formula is the stated consequence in settings where `1-q` is invertible, including the indicated formal-power-series and rational-function settings; the universally quantified product identity specializes to those settings and yields that consequence. No extra mathematically contentful hypothesis is added.

The target quantifies exactly over a field and the relevant elements: `∀ {R : Type u_2} [inst : Field R] (n : ℕ) (q : R)`, matching “Over a field” with `n ∈ ℕ` and `q` an element of that field. Its implication `q ^ n ≠ 1 → AlgebraicCombinatorics.qInt n q ≠ 0` directly matches “if $q^n \neq 1$ then $[n]_q \neq 0$.” The dependency defines `qInt n q` as `∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, q ^ i`, i.e. $q^0+q^1+\cdots+q^{n-1}$, exactly the informal definition of $[n]_q$ after substituting the field element `q`.

The blueprint states: “For any $n\in\mathbb N$, we have $[n]_1=n$ and $[n]_1!=n!$.” The two signatures assert exactly these equalities for every `(n : ℕ)`: `qInt n 1 = ↑n` and `qFactorial n 1 = ↑n.factorial`. Their dependency bodies match the informal definitions: `qInt n q = ∑ i ∈ Finset.range n, q ^ i` is $q^0+\cdots+q^{n-1}$, while `qFactorial n q = ∏ i ∈ Finset.range n, qInt (i+1) q` is $[1]_q\cdots[n]_q$. The formal ambient binder `{R : Type u_1} [CommSemiring R]` is more general than the section’s fixed commutative ring setting, since it does not require additive inverses; this strengthening in generality is faithful. The casts `↑n` and `↑n.factorial` correctly interpret the natural number and factorial in the ambient semiring.

The target adds the mathematically substantive hypothesis `k ≤ n →`, whereas the blueprint says only: “Over a field, when $q$ is not a root of unity of order $\le k$,” followed by the identity; it does not impose `k ≤ n`. This makes the Lean theorem weaker by omitting the cases `k > n`. Those cases are expressible with the project definitions: `qBinomial` explicitly returns `0` when `k ≤ n` is false, while the numerator product contains `qInt (n - n) q = qInt 0 q = 0` when `k > n`, using natural subtraction. The root condition is faithfully encoded by `∀ i ∈ Finset.range k, q ^ (i + 1) ≠ 1`, and the quotient of products is equivalent over a field to the displayed product of quotients under that condition. To make the declaration faithful, remove the binder `k ≤ n →`; alternatively, the blueprint statement would need to explicitly restrict to `k ≤ n`.

The blueprint assumes a “weakly increasing tuple in {0,1,…,m}^k”; the formal binders encode exactly this as `f : Fin k → Fin (m + 1)` with `Monotone f`. The dependency defines the transpose by `fun k m f j => ⟨{i | ↑(f i) > m - 1 - ↑j}.card, ⋯⟩`, matching `g_j = # { i : f_i > m−1−j }`. Finally, the conclusion `transposeMonotone m k (transposeMonotone k m f) = f` states that applying this operation twice recovers the original tuple. Function equality is precisely entrywise recovery. No mathematically substantive extra hypothesis or narrowed quantifier is present.

The target states, with no extra hypotheses, `∀ (k m : ℕ) (f : Fin k → Fin (m + 1)), ∑ j, ↑(transposeMonotone k m f j) = ∑ i, ↑(f i)`, matching “The transpose operation preserves the sum of values: ∑ j g(j) = ∑ i f(i).” Although the dependency defines `g(j) = #{i : f(i) > m - 1 - j}` rather than the informal convention `λᵗ_j = #{i : λ_i > j}`, this merely reverses the `Fin m` indexing of the transpose. Summing over all `j` is invariant under that reversal, so the asserted sum is the same transpose-size identity. The absence of a monotonicity/partition hypothesis makes the Lean theorem strictly more general: the layer-counting identity holds for every bounded `f : Fin k → Fin (m + 1)`, and hence in particular for the partitions contemplated by the blueprint.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.re.justification: The two definitions exactly implement the two directions. `removePartCopies` takes `p : n.Partition` and `j ≤ Multiset.count d p.parts`, matching “a partition p of n contains j or more copies of a part d,” and returns `(n - d * j).Partition`, matching the claimed resulting size. Its binder `d > 0` is justified by calling `d` a “part,” since the informal definition requires all partition parts to be positive. Conversely, `addPartCopies` takes `q : m.Partition`, `d j : ℕ`, and `d > 0`, and returns `(m + d * j).Partition`, exactly matching “adding j copies of a positive integer d … yields a partition of m + d · j.” The bodies use `Multiset.replicate j d` and multiset addition/subtraction, which encode adding or removing precisely `j` indistinguishable copies. Representing weakly decreasing tuples as multisets preserves the mathematical notion of partition.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.so.justification: The formal binders exactly encode the stated setting: `∀ {sl : List ℕ}, List.Pairwise (fun x1 x2 => x1 ≥ x2) sl → ∀ (j : ℕ) (hj : j < sl.length) (i : ℕ)` corresponds to “a sorted decreasing list ℓ,” “indices j < |ℓ|,” and “any i ∈ ℕ.” The conclusion `List.countP (fun x => decide (x > i)) sl > j ↔ sl[j] > i` says precisely that the number of entries exceeding `i` is greater than `j` iff the `j`-th entry exceeds `i`. `hj` supplies the validity proof for list indexing. Although the surrounding partition definition requires positive parts, the informal theorem itself only assumes a sorted decreasing list; in any event, allowing arbitrary natural entries would make the formal theorem more general, not weaker.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.su.justification: The blueprint’s definitions make a partition an “N-tuple … of nonnegative integers” of fixed length N and size n, whereas the target binds `(s : Finset n.Partition)`. By the base-library definition, `Nat.Partition n` consists of multisets of positive integers summing to n; it has no N parameter and omits the padded zero entries. Consequently, `Multiset.count d p.parts` is not the blueprint’s count among all N tuple entries, especially for `d = 0`, which the blueprint permits through “any d ∈ ℕ”. For example, zeros in an N-partition contribute to the informal count but can never occur in `p.parts`. The target also sums over `Finset.range (n + 1)` with threshold `j + 1`, hence thresholds 1 through n+1, while the blueprint explicitly sums from 1 through n. The extra term is harmless for `Nat.Partition` because its positive parts have multiplicity at most n, but it is not generally harmless for counts of zero entries in an N-tuple. To be faithful, the declaration must bind N, take `s` to be a finite set of weakly decreasing N-tuples of nonnegative integers of size n, count d among all N entries, and use thresholds 1 through n (e.g. `j ∈ Finset.range n` with threshold `j + 1`). Notably, with the supplied blueprint definitions the stated identity is itself false for unrestricted `d = 0` (for instance an all-zero tuple when n = 0), but it is still a statable proposition; the present declaration states a different, true identity for ordinary positive-part partitions.

The target quantifies over exactly the relevant data, `∀ {α : Type u_1} (s : Finset α) (p : α → Prop)`, and states `∑ x ∈ s, IversonBracket.iverson (p x) = (Finset.filter p s).card`. By the dependency body, `iverson (p x)` is `if p x then 1 else 0`, matching the informal bracket `[p(x)]`; its result is inferred as `ℕ` from the equality with `Finset.card`. By the library definition, `Finset.filter p s` is precisely the elements of `s` satisfying `p`, so its card is `|s ∩ {x : p(x)}|`. The binder `[inst : DecidablePred p]` is computational encoding needed for the conditional and filter, not a mathematically contentful extra hypothesis. Although the informal definition calls the truth value an integer, using naturals for a sum of values in `{0,1}` and comparing it with a natural cardinality faithfully expresses the stated equality.

The blueprint quantifies over “any partition p of n,” matching `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition)`. By the library docstrings, `p.parts : Multiset ℕ` contains the positive parts of the partition, `p.parts.sum` is their sum, `p.parts.toFinset` removes duplicates and therefore indexes exactly the distinct parts, and `Multiset.count d p.parts` is the multiplicity of `d`. Thus `∑ d ∈ p.parts.toFinset, d * Multiset.count d p.parts` is precisely the sum over distinct parts of each part weighted by its count. The implicit `DecidableEq ℕ` used by `toFinset` and `count` is only computational encoding and introduces no mathematical restriction.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.sy.justification: The five declarations exactly formalize the five listed properties using the dependency body `ℓ ::ₘ Multiset.map (fun x => ↑x + 1) ↑s`. Positivity is stated under the blueprint’s assumption `∀ ℓ ≥ 1 ... 0 < x`. Cardinality is `(symToPartsMultiset✝ ℓ s).card = n + 1`, which becomes `k` when `n = k - 1` and `k ≥ 1`. The largest-part claim is `Multiset.fold max 0 ... = ℓ`. Erasure is exactly `(symToPartsMultiset✝ ℓ s).erase ℓ = Multiset.map (fun x => ↑x + 1) ↑s`; this remains correct even when a mapped part also equals `ℓ`, since erasing one occurrence removes the distinguished consed occurrence up to multiset equality. Finally, for `s : Sym (Fin ℓ) (k - 1)`, the sum theorem assumes `k ≥ 1` and `ℓ ≥ 1` and concludes membership in `Finset.Icc k (k * ℓ)`, exactly the interval `[k, kℓ]`. The cardinality, maximum, and erasure declarations are stated more generally using arbitrary `n` (and the maximum/erasure claims do not require `ℓ ≥ 1`), which strengthens rather than weakens the blueprint statement.

stmt-algebraic-combinatorics-lem.pars.tr.justification: The target quantifies over every natural size and partition, `{n : ℕ} → n.Partition → n.Partition`, matching “For any partition λ.” Its body sets `largest := Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, then ranges over `Finset.range largest`, i.e. zero-based indices `i = 0, …, p-1`, and assigns each entry `(Multiset.filter (fun x => x > i) p.parts).card`. Under the index shift from formal `i` to the blueprint’s one-based index `i+1`, `x > i` for naturals is exactly `x ≥ i+1`, so this matches `μ_i = # of parts … that are ≥ i` for `i ∈ {1,…,p}`. The return type is again `n.Partition`; since `Nat.Partition` consists of positive parts summing to `n`, this encodes `|λᵗ| = |λ|`. Using a multiset rather than an explicitly weakly decreasing tuple is a representation choice, not a mathematical restriction, and the generated counts are the conjugate partition’s parts.

The target quantifies over every natural size and every partition, `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition)`, and concludes exactly `p.transpose.transpose = p`, matching “$(\lambda^t)^t=\lambda$ for every partition $\lambda$.” The project representation—`Nat.Partition` as a multiset of positive integers summing to `n`—forgets only the forced weakly decreasing presentation of a partition, not mathematical information. Its transpose body counts, for each `i < largest`, the parts satisfying `x > i`, which agrees with the informal definition that the `i`-th transposed part is the number of original parts exceeding `i` (with zero-based indexing). Quantifying over `n : ℕ` introduces no substantive restriction because a finite tuple of positive integers necessarily has nonnegative size. The formal theorem also includes the empty partition of size zero, which is at most a harmless generalization.

The blueprint says “largest part of λᵗ = ℓ(λ).” The target states exactly `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition), p.transpose.largestPart = p.numParts`. Here `p.numParts` is `p.parts.card`, matching the informal length `m`, while `transpose` forms the parts `#{x ∈ p.parts : x > i}` over `i < largest`, matching the informal formula `|{j : j < N, λ_j > i}|`. Finally, `largestPart` is the maximum of those parts. The formal theorem also covers the empty partition using the declared convention that its largest part is `0`; this is a harmless extension beyond the informal transpose definition’s `N > 0` requirement, not a weakening of the blueprint claim.

The target states for every `{n : ℕ}` and `p : n.Partition` that `p.transpose.numParts = p.largestPart`, exactly matching “The length of the transpose equals the largest part of the original partition.” Here `numParts` is `p.parts.card`, which is the partition’s length, and `largestPart` is `Multiset.fold max 0 p.parts`, the largest part. The body of `transpose` creates one candidate part for each `i` in `Finset.range largest`, with value `#{x ∈ p.parts | x > i}`, matching the informal definition that the transpose has parts counting original parts exceeding `i`. For every `i < largest`, this count is positive, so the final zero filter does not shorten the resulting partition; hence its number of parts is `largest`. The formal theorem also covers the empty partition using largest part `0`; this is a harmless stronger/general extension beyond the informal transpose definition’s `N > 0` setting.

The blueprint states “The transpose preserves size: |λᵗ| = |λ|, i.e., if λ is a partition of n, then λᵗ is also a partition of n.” The elaborated target quantifies over exactly such data, `∀ {n : ℕ} (p : n.Partition)`, and concludes `p.transpose.parts.sum = n`. Since `Nat.Partition.parts` are positive integers summing to the partition’s index, this equality says `|pᵗ| = n = |p|`. Moreover, `Nat.Partition.transpose : {n : ℕ} → n.Partition → n.Partition` already ensures at the type level that the transpose is a partition of the same `n`. Its body computes, for each `i ∈ Finset.range largest`, `(Multiset.filter (fun x => x > i) p.parts).card`, matching the informal definition that the `i`-th transposed part counts original parts exceeding `i`.
